claims.claim: RSC is strongly and ubiquitously engaged during fMRI studies of recalling autobiographical memories.
claims.source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claims.claim: RSC is strongly and ubiquitously engaged during fMRI studies of imagining future and fictitious events.
claims.source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claims.claim: All of scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory, and imagining future events involve picturing scenes or events, with RSC possibly signalling the presence of permanent features.
claims.source: All of these involve picturing scenes or events, with RSC possibly signalling the presence of permanent features (Auger and Maguire, 2013).
claims.evidence: The authors propose this interpretation based on their findings and prior work.

claims.claim: Otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks.
claims.source: Auger et al. (2012) and Auger and Maguire (2013) found that otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks, and had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Poor navigators had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
claims.source: Auger et al. (2012) and Auger and Maguire (2013) found that otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks, and had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Damage involving the RSC leaves patients unable to derive orientation information from landmarks which they can otherwise recognise.
claims.source: In neuropsychological studies, damage involving the RSC is never focal, but nevertheless leaves patients unable to derive orientation information from landmarks which they can otherwise recognise (Maguire, 2001a; Vann et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior neuropsychological studies.

claims.claim: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC.
claims.source: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC (Villain et al., 2008; Pengas et al., 2010, 2012; Tu et al., 2015), and spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of the disease.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claims.claim: Spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of Alzheimer's Disease.
claims.source: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC (Villain et al., 2008; Pengas et al., 2010, 2012; Tu et al., 2015), and spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of the disease.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on clinical knowledge about Alzheimer's Disease.

claims.claim: If representations of space are founded upon permanence information from RSC, then it needs to be dependable.
claims.source: If representations of space are founded upon permanence information from RSC, as seems to be indicated by our results, then it needs to be dependable.
claims.evidence: The authors propose this logical inference based on their findings.

claims.claim: If RSC permanence information is not dependable, afflicted individuals may be falling at the first hurdle, and one can understand why spatial disorientation then arises.
claims.source: If this is not the case, afflicted individuals may be falling at the first hurdle, so to speak, and one can understand why spatial disorientation then arises, because upstream regions that rely on good quality input cannot perform optimally to build reliable environmental representations.
claims.evidence: The authors speculate about the implications of RSC dysfunction.

claims.claim: The current results provide compelling evidence that the RSC may be fundamentally concerned with coding for permanent landmarks.
claims.source: We believe that the current results provide compelling evidence that the RSC may be fundamentally concerned with coding for permanent landmarks.
claims.evidence: The authors state their interpretation of their findings.

claims.claim: RSC coding for permanent landmarks may account for its involvement in scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory and future-thinking, providing input for upstream areas such as the hippocampus to then construct models of the world based upon reliable cues.
claims.source: We further propose that this may account for its involvement in scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory and future-thinking, providing input for upstream areas such as the hippocampus to then construct models of the world based upon reliable cues (Maguire and Mullally, 2013; Zeidman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The authors propose this model based on their findings and cite related theoretical work.

claims.claim: Ten subjects took part in a landmark characterisation study.
claims.source: Ten subjects (five female, mean age 28 years, SD 4.8) took part in a landmark characterisation study.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claims.claim: None of the landmark characterisation subjects took part in the subsequent fMRI study.
claims.source: None of these subjects took part in the subsequent fMRI study.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claims.claim: 134 unique 3D 'alien' items were created to be used as potential landmarks in Fog World.
claims.source: We created 134 unique 3D 'alien' items to be used as potential landmarks in Fog World (examples in Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods and reference Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Two groups of 30 landmarks each were selected from the original set of 134 to be used as the permanent and transient landmarks within the VR environment.
claims.source: Using these ratings, we selected two groups of 30 landmarks each (from the original set of 134) to be used as the permanent and transient landmarks within the VR environment.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claims.claim: The two landmark groups did not differ in terms of salience, other associations, likeableness, animateness, or memorableness.
claims.source: These object groups were carefully selected to ensure that they did not differ in terms of any of the features rated (t-tests of the two landmark groups: Salience: t58 = 0.669, p = 0.51; Other associations: t58 = 0.000, p = 1.0; Likeableness: t58 = 0.312, p = 0.76; Animateness: t58 = −1.089, p = 0.28; Memorableness: t58 = 0.247, p = 0.81).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of landmark features.

claims.claim: The landmark groups did not differ in actual size or mean spatial frequency.
claims.source: The landmarks groups did not differ on two other factors—the actual size of the items (when in the VR environment: Small/Medium/Large; [t58 = 0.000, p = 1.0] and mean spatial frequency [t58 = −0.562, p = 0.58]).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of landmark features.

claims.claim: 32 different subjects took part in the fMRI study.
claims.source: 32 different subjects (16 female, mean age 23.7 years, SD 2.4) took part in the fMRI study.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claims.claim: Fog World was created using the jMonkeyEngine 3.0 beta game engine, Java JDK 1.6 and Blender.
claims.source: Fog World was created using the jMonkeyEngine 3.0 beta game engine (http://jmonkeyengine.org), Java JDK 1.6 (Sun Microsystems, Santa Clara, California) and Blender (Stichting Blender Foundation, Amsterdam).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claims.claim: There were 60 trials in total, with the five paths being travelled 12 times each.
claims.source: There were 60 trials in total, with the five paths being travelled 12 times each (i.e., once per learning sweep).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: Permanent landmarks remained in the same location on each trial, whereas transient landmarks appeared in a different location on every exposure.
claims.source: Permanent landmarks remained in the same location on each trial, whereas transient landmarks appeared in a different location on every exposure.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: The permanent and transient landmarks were placed in equivalent locations within the environment.
claims.source: The locations in which all 60 landmarks appeared on each of the 60 trials were meticulously designed so that permanent and transient landmarks were equally distributed either side and along the whole length of each path. This ensured that the permanent and transient landmarks, as well as being matched for their perceptual features (size, visual salience, and other features—see above), were placed in equivalent locations within the environment.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design to control for confounds.

claims.claim: Each video took a first person perspective travelling along one of the paths.
claims.source: Each video took a first person perspective travelling along one of the paths.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: When a landmark emerged out of the fog, the camera turned to bring the landmark into the centre of the screen, where it was positioned for 2 s.
claims.source: On each trial, the camera travelled along a path in a straight line. When a landmark emerged out of the fog, the camera turned to bring the landmark into the centre of the screen, where it was positioned for 2 s, the camera then panned back to the middle of the path as it continued travelling forwards (Figure 2A from top to bottom; see also Video 1).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and reference Figure 2A and Video 1.

claims.claim: The paths were always travelled in the same direction, with the same start and end point each time.
claims.source: The paths were always travelled in the same direction, with the same start and end point each time.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: Each path intersected with two others.
claims.source: To encourage subjects to learn an integrated representation of the whole environment, the paths intersected one another. Each path intersected with two others (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and reference Figure 1C.

claims.claim: These 60 videos were each approximately 1 min in length.
claims.source: These 60 videos (corresponding to the 60 trials) were each approximately 1 min in length.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: There were a total of 12 learning sweeps throughout the experiment.
claims.source: There were a total of 12 learning sweeps throughout the experiment (divided into four scanning runs, or 'quarters', comprising three sweeps each).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claims.claim: Each 3-sweep scanning run lasted 15–20 min.
claims.source: Each 3-sweep scanning run lasted 15–20 min and subjects could take a short break (while remaining in the scanner) between scanning runs when necessary.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their experimental procedure.

claims.claim: A Bayesian implementation of a 'state-space' model provided the best fit to the learning data.
claims.source: Of the models tested (see 'Materials and methods') a Bayesian implementation of a 'state-space' model provided the best fit to the data (Smith et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claims.claim: T2*-weighted single-shot echo-planar images with BOLD contrast were acquired on a 3T Magnetom Allegra head-only MRI scanner.
claims.source: T2*-weighted single-shot echo-planar images with BOLD contrast were acquired on a 3T Magnetom Allegra head-only MRI scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) operated with the standard transmit-receive head coil.
claims.evidence: The authors describe their scanning parameters.

claims.claim: FMRI data were analysed using SPM8.
claims.source: FMRI data were analysed using SPM8 (www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm).
claims.evidence: The authors describe their analysis methods.

results.result: Multiple brain areas including hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, parahippocampal cortex, retrosplenial cortex, and posterior parietal cortex have been implicated in spatial representation and navigation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by extensive citations to prior research across multiple species. These claims establish the background knowledge about brain regions involved in spatial navigation, which is appropriately documented through literature review.

results.result: There is a gap in knowledge about how environmental representations evolve de novo in humans, particularly when no prior experience of key elements exists.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C11 identify a research gap based on the authors' literature review. While these are inference-based claims about what has not been studied, they are appropriately supported by the review of existing work (C7-C10) and establish the rationale for the current study.

results.result: The permanent and transient landmark groups were carefully matched across multiple features including visual salience, memorableness, size, spatial frequency, and other characteristics through an initial characterization study with separate subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C119-C124 describe the landmark characterization procedure with appropriate statistical validation (t-tests showing no significant differences between groups). This experimental control is well-documented and critical for the study design.

results.result: Participants learned to recognize permanent and transient landmarks at similar overall rates, though there was a transient advantage for permanent landmarks in the second and third quarters, with equal recognition by the first and final quarters.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (linear regression, repeated measures ANOVA with interaction, paired t-tests) with reported statistics and p-values. The pattern shows initial equivalence, temporary divergence, then convergence, which is clearly documented.

results.result: Post-scan testing confirmed that participants successfully learned landmark features, with no difference in recognition of permanent versus transient landmarks, high accuracy for novel landmark identification, and strong correlations between ratings and actual values for permanence and size.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by statistical analyses showing non-significant differences where expected and significant correlations (r=0.793 for permanence, r=0.726 for size) where appropriate. This validates that learning occurred successfully.

results.result: Visual salience of landmarks was influenced by their experience within the environment, and factor analysis confirmed four independent components of landmark features including permanence as a distinct factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by correlation analyses and principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation. The factor analysis appropriately identified four orthogonal factors accounting for 96.4% of variance, with permanence loading strongly on factor 1.

results.result: Navigation task performance showed substantial variance across participants, with evidence that participants were learning integrated spatial knowledge rather than simple associations, though only 2 of 32 participants explicitly focused on landmark permanence.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis. The variance (mean=12.8, SD=8.1) and scoring pattern analysis (t31=-2.121, p=0.042) support the interpretation, while debriefing data confirms the incidental nature of permanence learning.

results.result: fMRI analysis revealed that permanent landmarks elicited greater activation than transient landmarks in RSC, POS, PHC, hippocampus, and occipital regions, with these differences emerging by the third quarter in RSC and POS, but not until the final quarter in hippocampus and PHC.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by whole-brain fMRI analyses with appropriate statistical thresholds (p<0.05 FWE corrected, with some results at p<0.0001 uncorrected). The temporal progression of activation is clearly documented with coordinates and Z-scores, showing RSC/POS engagement before hippocampus/PHC.

results.result: Parametric fMRI analysis using permanence factor scores showed increasing activation in RSC, POS, PHC, and other regions across learning, with bilateral RSC and POS activation in the final quarter and hippocampus/PHC activation at reduced threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by parametric fMRI analyses using orthogonalized factor scores from PCA. The analyses appropriately use continuous regressors and report activations with coordinates and Z-scores, converging with the categorical analyses in C39-C44.

results.result: The memorableness factor was associated with activation in POS, occipital, parietal, temporal cortices, and RSC across the whole session, with POS showing greater response to memorable landmarks in the first quarter but no activation in the final quarter, indicating a switch from memorable to permanent landmark processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by parametric fMRI analyses and are illustrated in Figure 5. The temporal switch in POS responsivity from memorableness to permanence is a key finding, well-documented with appropriate statistics and visualization of the response profiles.

results.result: Size and visual salience factors showed constant responses in posterior visual areas throughout learning, while RSC developed permanence representations, POS initially responded to memorable then permanent landmarks, and hippocampus/PHC engaged with stable items later and less strongly.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 summarize the fMRI findings across all four factors. These summary claims are well-supported by the detailed analyses in C39-C52 and appropriately synthesize the temporal and regional patterns of activation.

results.result: RSC activity directly tracked individual subjects' learning of landmark permanence, with the permanence representation being graded rather than binary, relating to the precision of permanence knowledge.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59, C70, C79-C81 are supported by subject-specific learning model analyses using Bayesian state-space models (C137). The RSC activation (9, -58, 22; Z=4.38) correlating with individual learning curves provides strong evidence for RSC's role in encoding permanence knowledge with graded precision.

results.result: In the second half of learning, both RSC and POS showed increased functional connectivity with anterior hippocampus when viewing permanent versus transient landmarks, with connectivity strength related to permanence learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by PPI connectivity analyses with appropriate seed regions and contrasts. The emergence of RSC-hippocampus and POS-hippocampus connectivity only in the second half of learning, with coordinates and Z-scores reported, demonstrates the development of network interactions during learning.

results.result: MVB analysis revealed that only hippocampus, and only in the final quarter, contained multi-voxel patterns related to knowledge of permanent landmark locations, while RSC, POS, and PHC did not show such representations at any point.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C89 are supported by MVB decoding analyses with appropriate model evidence thresholds (log evidence=12.8, posterior probability=1.0) and permutation testing (p=0.0396). This demonstrates a dissociation between RSC's permanence coding and hippocampus's location coding.

results.result: RSC played a central and highly selective role by representing only the most stable, permanent features, followed by increased RSC-hippocampus coupling and hippocampal expression of permanent landmark locations and environmental layout.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69, C117 synthesize the main findings from the fMRI, connectivity, and MVB analyses. These high-level conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analysis approaches (C39-C66) showing RSC's selective permanence coding and its relationship to hippocampal spatial representations.

results.result: RSC developed robust and selective sensitivity to stable landmarks rapidly (by the third quarter), showing remarkable adaptability and specificity by not responding to other features when permanence information was unavailable.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by the temporal progression of RSC activation (C43-C44, C47) and comparison with POS (C52). The specificity is demonstrated by RSC's lack of response to other factors (C53) and its contrast with POS's initial memorableness response. C73 is supported by prior work citations.

results.result: RSC and POS are cytoarchitecturally distinct with different connectivity patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by citation to anatomical literature (Vann et al., 2009) and serves as justification for treating these regions separately rather than as a 'retrosplenial complex.' This is appropriate given the functional differences observed in the current study.

results.result: RSC may indicate reliability of spatial representations based on permanence, while POS may index navigational utility or relate landmarks to discrete locations, with POS representations being more local compared to hippocampal representations of overall layout.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C84-C86, C90 are speculative interpretations of the functional roles of RSC and POS. While these interpretations are reasonable given the data (C79-C81 for RSC, C51-C52 for POS), they extend beyond what is directly demonstrated and are appropriately presented as possibilities requiring future investigation.

results.result: Unlike RSC which tracked permanence knowledge acquisition, hippocampus was only engaged by landmarks that were both known to be permanent and associated with a specific place.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by the contrast between RSC's correlation with learning state (C58-C59) and hippocampus's later emergence (C42, C48, C65) and location-specific coding (C65-C66). This demonstrates a functional dissociation between permanence coding and spatial location coding.

results.result: RSC may code for environmental feature stability and provide input to hippocampus for building spatial representations, consistent with anatomical connectivity between RSC and medial temporal lobes and prior findings of RSC-hippocampus interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C97 integrate the current findings with anatomical and functional literature. C92-C97 are well-supported by citations to anatomical and physiological studies. C91 is a reasonable synthesis of the current connectivity findings (C60-C62) with this anatomical knowledge, though it remains a proposed model.

results.result: The current findings provide an alternative interpretation of prior work on RSC and spatial judgments, suggesting RSC activity reflects fundamental permanence representation rather than coding space relative to landmarks, which may anchor spatial representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 appropriately reinterpret prior findings (Committeri et al., 2004; Sulpizio et al., 2013) in light of the current results. This reinterpretation is reasonable given the strong evidence for RSC permanence coding (C67-C81), though C102 includes speculative elements about functional implications.

results.result: Head direction cells have been found in rodent RSC but account for only approximately 8% of cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by citations to prior animal studies (Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001). This contextualizes the current findings by noting that most RSC cells have unknown functions, motivating investigation of permanence coding.

results.result: RSC's discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks may explain its engagement during scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory, and future thinking, with RSC possibly signaling permanent features in these contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are speculative extensions of the current findings to explain RSC's role in other cognitive domains. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations showing RSC engagement in these tasks, the direct link between permanence coding and these functions requires empirical validation.

results.result: Poor navigators have difficulty identifying permanent landmarks and show reduced RSC responses, RSC damage impairs deriving orientation from landmarks, and RSC shows early changes in Alzheimer's disease where spatial disorientation is an early symptom.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 are supported by citations to prior clinical and neuropsychological studies. These claims contextualize the current findings by showing the importance of RSC permanence processing for navigation and the consequences of RSC dysfunction.

results.result: If spatial representations are founded on RSC permanence information, then unreliable RSC input could cause spatial disorientation by preventing upstream regions from building reliable environmental representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are logical inferences from the current findings (C67-C91) and clinical observations (C112-C114), but remain speculative. The proposed causal chain from RSC permanence coding to spatial disorientation is plausible but requires direct empirical testing.

results.result: RSC coding for permanent landmarks may account for its involvement in scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory and future-thinking, providing input for hippocampus to construct world models based on reliable cues.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 proposes a comprehensive model of RSC function based on the current findings. While this synthesis is reasonable given the evidence for RSC permanence coding (C67-C81) and RSC-hippocampus connectivity (C60-C62), the extension to multiple cognitive domains requires additional empirical support.

results.result: The fMRI study used 32 subjects, a custom VR environment with controlled landmark exposure through fog, 60 trials across 12 learning sweeps in four quarters, with careful control of landmark locations and exposure, and standard fMRI acquisition and analysis procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C136, C138-C139 describe the experimental methods in detail. These methodological claims are well-documented and appropriate for the research question. The sample size (n=32) is reasonable for fMRI, and the experimental controls (fog, matched locations, controlled exposure) are well-justified.

results.result: A Bayesian state-space model provided the best fit to learning data compared to alternative models.
results.evaluation: Claim C137 is supported by model comparison using appropriate metrics (MSE and r²). The Bayesian state-space model showed superior performance (MSE=204, r²=64) compared to maximum likelihood (MSE=226, r²=44) and moving average (MSE=221, r²=36) approaches, justifying its use for subject-specific analyses.

results.result: Prior work showed PHC responds to visuospatial features while RSC responds to permanent landmarks, suggesting RSC codes for permanent landmarks to build stable spatial representations, though previous studies used familiar landmarks.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 accurately summarize prior findings (Auger et al., 2012; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Konkle and Oliva, 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Marchette et al., 2014; Troiani et al., 2014) and identify a limitation (familiar landmarks) that motivates the current study's use of novel landmarks.

results.result: Object-centered firing has been observed in rodent lateral entorhinal and anterior cingulate cortex, even for formerly occupied locations.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by citations to animal studies (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2012; Weible et al., 2012; Tsao et al., 2013). This contextualizes the lack of findings in other regions in the current study and suggests directions for future research.
